sentences.text: Mina visits her grandmother every Sunday for tea.
Grandmother lives in a small house beside the park.
The kitchen opens onto a bright room with a blue table.
This Sunday, Grandmother plans to share tea with her old neighbor Lan.
Lan lives across town now, but she still loves their tea talks.
Mina hangs her coat on a hook and joins Grandmother in the kitchen.
Grandmother takes a blue tin from the shelf and sets it on the table.
"Lan likes plain tea," she says.
"She takes no milk or sugar with her tea."
Mina reads the label on the tin, though she knows the tea by its smell.
They wash two cups and place them on a tray.
Grandmother fills a kettle and puts it on the stove.
Mina asks how many leaves fit in each tea cup.
"A small spoon works well for one tea cup," Grandmother says.
Mina takes the spoon and counts two small heaps of tea.
A few leaves fall on the table.
She laughs as tea leaves fall around the cup.
Mina sweeps the dry leaves into a bin on the floor.
As the kettle warms, they talk about Lan and the old tea stall.
Grandmother met Lan at that stall by the school gate over tea.
They sat at the stall after class and shared one cup of tea.
After many years apart, Lan visits again for tea.
Mina wonders if Lan remembers their long talks over tea.
A clock on the wall says eleven.
The tea is hot, but Grandmother lifts the kettle from the stove.
She waits a short time before pouring, because a rolling boil can make green tea bitter.
Mina watches tea fill each cup, one at a time.
The pale tea smells fresh and light.
Grandmother asks Mina to carry the tray into the front room.
Mina holds the tray with both hands and walks slowly across the room.
A soft knock sounds on the door.
Lan stands at the door with an umbrella and a bag of tea.
Her hair is wet, but the tea stays warm on the tray.
Lan smiles when she sees Grandmother in the front room.
They hug by the door, then sit at the table and pour tea.
Lan puts her bag on the chair and opens it.
Inside, Lan keeps a small photo of the old stall on the table.
"I found it in my desk last week," Lan says.
Mina looks at the first photo on top.
Two young women sit at a tea stall and laugh.
Grandmother and Lan look just as happy in the picture.
Mina pours tea for Lan, then takes a seat by the window.
Lan lifts the cup and smells the tea before she drinks.
"The tea has the same soft taste," she says.
Grandmother asks what tea Lan makes in her new flat.
Lan tells them about her garden and tea with a neighbor.
Mina listens while she drinks her tea.
The story makes the room feel bright, even as rain taps on the window.
Lan asks Mina which books she reads, and Mina answers over tea.
Mina tells her about a book while the tea cools on the table.
Lan knows that story, too, and names the next book while rain taps on the window.
Mina writes the title on a paper strip beside her tea cup.
The women share tea and talk about small things for a long time.
No one checks the clock on the wall.
When the tea is gone, Grandmother offers another cup.
Lan says yes to another cup of tea, and Mina prepares it.
She measures the tea leaves, waits for the kettle, and pours slowly.
The tea is not too strong this time.
Lan says Mina makes a fine cup of tea.
Mina feels proud of the tea, but she knows she can learn more.
Before Lan leaves, they set a day for the next tea visit.
She takes the old photos but leaves one on the table for Mina.
Mina puts the photo in her school bag beside the paper strip with the book title.
The rain ends, and sun comes into the room.
Lan waves from the gate as Mina stands in the doorway.
Mina clears the cups and washes the tea pot.
Grandmother says the visit and shared tea make the day special.
Mina asks if she can make tea again next Sunday.
Grandmother nods and saves the blue tin on the shelf.
On Mina's walk across town, she thinks about Lan's stories and tea.
She knows how to make the tea now, but she likes the talk best.
After the visit, she tells her mother about Lan over one more cup of tea.
Jo takes a small coffee to the cafe window and opens her folder.
She has one hour to finish a poster in the cafe before lunch.
The garden group needs the poster on Saturday.
Jo sketches rows of vegetables, a path, and a bright sun while her coffee waits beside the page.
The words in the picture look plain, though the drawing feels good.
Jo takes a sip, then checks the date on the page.
The coffee cup rests far from the paper, so Jo can draw without worry.
She writes the date in large letters and checks each line.
A woman at the next table asks what Jo is drawing beside her coffee.
Jo explains the garden idea as she takes a sip of coffee.
The woman offers to bring small pots for the garden, and Jo writes that in the margin.
Jo adds a note about the pots in the open space.
The coffee scent reminds Jo to pause and look at her own cup.
Her coffee is still warm, so she drinks before returning to the poster.
Jo notices a small wobble in the table when she moves her arm.
She places her folder in the center and steadies the paper.
A child runs past, and coffee shivers inside Jo's cup.
Jo catches her coffee, but a few drops land on the poster.
The coffee marks spread across the corner and cross part of the sun.
Jo feels upset because coffee stains the sun and the garden path.
She asks the cafe worker for a clean cloth and a new sheet to save the coffee poster.
The worker brings both, then sets another coffee on a side shelf.
She dabs the paper, but the coffee stain blurs the ink.
Jo takes a slow breath and studies the brown circle on the page.
The ring could pass for a sun above the garden rows on the page.
She turns the coffee-marked page and sees a new idea.
Jo draws a larger sun around the ring, then adds rays on the page.
The stain now fits in the design.
The worker says the coffee sun will brighten the poster.
Jo writes a new heading in the space above the picture.
The heading invites people to bring a cup and meet in the garden.
The woman in the next chair reads the poster and points to one detail.
She says the date should stand out in the coffee-colored picture.
Jo makes the hour larger and moves the date down on the page.
A man at the door suggests a small map in the bottom corner.
Jo adds the cafe and garden gate to the map in the bottom corner.
The coffee grows cool while she draws, but she does not mind.
Jo takes another sip of coffee and checks the whole poster.
The path on the map leads from the street to the garden.
Jo adds a place for bags on the map beside the garden path.
The woman sets down her coffee and offers Jo a green pencil.
Jo colors the garden rows beside the coffee sun.
The green makes the poster feel calm, and the coffee ring gives it warmth.
Jo copies the final design of the coffee sun onto a clean sheet.
She keeps the first page in her folder as a reminder of the mistake.
The cafe worker clears the table where Jo first spilled coffee.
Jo writes the last line in the cafe and checks every letter.
The poster says neighbors can plant, share lunch, and learn together over coffee.
Jo takes a photo of the poster in the cafe window and sends it to the garden leader.
The garden leader reads the message in Jo's photo and asks her to bring it over.
Jo folds the folder around the poster and finishes her coffee.
On the way to the garden, Jo passes the cafe window and sees her coffee poster in the glass.
Jo walks two blocks with the poster held flat under her arm, smiling at the coffee ring.
The garden crew has coffee in paper cups beside the tools and small pots.
She pins the poster on the garden gate beside the cups.
The garden leader sees the coffee sun and laughs with delight.
The garden leader says the ring gives the picture warmth on the page.
Jo tells her how the spill became part of the design on the page.
They place the extra copy in the cafe window for people to see.
Later, Jo returns to the cafe and orders one small coffee.
She sits in the cafe, opens her folder, and writes down the day's story.
Coffee tastes richer after Jo finishes the poster.
Jo watches the garden gate from the cafe window, coffee cup in hand.
The sun on the page seems to shine over the real garden.
On Saturday, she brings a watering can to the first planting day.
The garden group meets on the path by the poster as Jo helps a child plant beans.
They share lunch after planting, and the leader saves Jo a cup of coffee.
Jo thinks the best part is not the coffee or the poster alone.
In the garden, she sees neighbors make a place together.
Linh volunteers at a hill garden where water comes from a spring above town.
The garden sends herbs and vegetables to the food center in town.
During a dry summer, the water flow becomes weak at the garden tap.
On hot days, the leaves curl although the beds still look green.
Linh checks the schedule on the wall and sees that the spring should supply the garden.
She asks Bao, the caretaker, to walk the route with her on the hillside.
Bao brings a map, a wrench, and a small notebook for notes on their walk.
On their map, they trace a pipe from the tap to a covered tank.
Water reaches the tap through a pipe from a covered tank.
The tank sits on a slope; gravity carries its flow downhill.
Linh marks each junction on the map as they climb.
A narrow channel carries water along the stone path toward the garden.
After a turn, they hear water running beneath a wooden cover.
The sound of water grows stronger below the bridge.
Bao lifts the cover over the water pipe with a tool while Linh holds it steady.
A loose joint lets water escape into the soil.
The water leak is small, but it runs all day.
Bao closes the water valve before touching the pipe.
Linh calls the town crew to report the water leak.
A repair worker arrives with a new seal and checks the water pipe.
He asks Linh to read the water meter while Bao turns the valve.
The numbers stay still when the water is off.
The worker fits the seal, then lets water into the pipe a little at a time.
Water moves through the pipe without a leak.
The meter turns as water reaches the lower channel.
Linh watches the water pass under the bridge and into the garden tank.
They wait to see whether water pressure stays steady.
At first, the water tap gives only a thin stream.
The worker checks the water valve and finds leaves caught around its handle.
Bao clears the leaves, and water runs again.
Water flows from the garden tap with a stronger sound.
Linh fills a bottle and uses the extra water to test the pressure.
The worker asks Linh to check the water meter the next day.
He also asks them to report any new water leak quickly.
Linh adds both notes in the map's margin.
She marks the repaired joint with a red circle on the map.
They return to the square and explain how the repair restores water flow.
A sign on the gate asks people to use water with care.
Linh suggests adding a simple water map beside the sign.
The group agrees that visitors should know where the water comes from.
Bao draws the spring, tank, pipe, and garden on a large sheet.
Linh adds arrows to show the water flow direction.
The map helps people see that water connects the hill and the town.
One gardener asks if the spring will supply water through the summer.
Bao says the water level is steady, but everyone should avoid waste.
Linh explains that a slow pour gives plants time to take water.
The group places small cans beside the beds for careful water use.
They also check the water tap after each gardening session.
On a later day, rain falls on the hill for an hour.
The channel carries water under the bridge without rising above its sides.
Linh visits the garden the next day to read the meter on the tank.
The water meter is normal, and the ground beside the pipe stays dry.
She writes the reading in her notebook and tells Bao.
He smiles as water reaches the garden beds again.
The garden tap now fills several cans in a short time.
A child asks where the water line begins.
Linh follows the blue water line with a finger and explains the route.
Water starts above the houses, passes through the tank, and reaches the square.
From the square, another pipe brings water to the garden.
The child says the water route is longer than it looks.
Linh agrees and points to the marked joint on the map.
The garden group puts the map in a clear case by the gate.
In the garden, visitors pause to read the map before filling their bottles at the tap.
They discuss how even a small leak matters in a dry summer.
Linh returns with Bao to the spring where water starts its route.
They hear the stream run quietly in the clear channel.
They check the cover, both valves, and the tank on the hillside one last time.
Nothing needs repair along the water line after the check.
Linh walks back with the map in her hand.
She understands the system in greater detail, and she knows whom to call.
The plants stand upright in the garden after the rain.
The group shares a meal and fresh water, then talks about next season.
Linh fills a glass at the tap and sets it on the table.
She thinks about the path the water takes before it reaches her.
